page_intro: Historian of the Cold War, cultural diplomacy, and East-Central Europe at the University of Warsaw.
paragraphs: I am a historian at the University of Warsaw, where I study and teach the political and intellectual history of twentieth-century East-Central Europe, particularly Poland and Ukraine. I studied history in Kyiv and Warsaw, and much of my research has grown out of an interest in how the region’s history was understood, debated, and written on both sides of the Iron Curtain.

My first book, Rzeczpospolita uczonych (2024), grew out of my research on Ukrainian and Polish émigré scholars in the United States. I was interested not only in the ideas they developed but also in the institutions they built, the intellectual worlds they inhabited, and their efforts to challenge established ways of thinking about Eastern Europe. Intellectual history remains central to my work. I continue to explore Ukrainian political thought, the relationship between intellectual life in exile and dissent within Soviet Ukraine, and the emergence of East-Central Europe as a distinct field of knowledge in Cold War America.

Increasingly, I am also interested in the relationship between ideas and foreign policy: how intellectual debates influenced political thinking and how international politics, in turn, shaped those debates. This question informs two of my current projects: an edition of the correspondence between Jerzy Giedroyc and Zbigniew Brzezinski, and a study of the Paris-based Literary Institute (Instytut Literacki), its American connections, and its role in Cold War debates over the future of Eastern Europe.

Another major interest of mine is American cultural diplomacy, particularly academic exchange with communist Eastern Europe. My book on the Fulbright Program in Poland, published in Polish in 2024 and in English with Manchester University Press in 2026, examines how exchanges between Poland and the United States shaped bilateral relations over several generations.

More recently, I have also turned to the history of Ukrainian–Russian relations. I am particularly interested in Ukraine’s place within the Soviet system of power, the contradictions of Soviet federalism, and Ukraine’s importance to Russian conceptions of statehood and great-power status. Rather than approaching this history solely through the opposition between imperial domination and national resistance, I seek to understand the changing political relationship between Ukraine and Russia, both before and after the Soviet collapse.
Alongside my research and teaching, I take part in public discussions about the history of Eastern Europe, the Cold War, and the historical background of Russia’s war against Ukraine.
short_bio: Oleksandr Avramchuk is Assistant Professor at the Faculty of History, University of Warsaw. His research focuses on the modern history of East-Central Europe, particularly Polish-Ukrainian relations, Cold War diplomacy, and its post-1991 legacies. He also studies Soviet Ukraine, examining its relations with both the West and the centre of power in Moscow. He is the author of Rzeczpospolita uczonych. Powstanie studiów ukraińskich i polsko-ukraiński dialog historyków w Stanach Zjednoczonych, 1939–1991 (University of Warsaw Press, 2024) and A History of the Fulbright Program in Poland, 1945–2025: To Build a Republic of Spirit (Manchester University Press, 2026), and co-editor of Paradoks istnienia. Korespondencja Michała Łesiowa i Romana Szporluka, 1955–2016 (2026)
